title: The Hypernormalisation of Information Systems Research
affiliations: Victoria University of Wellington - Te Herenga Waka

detail.title: The Hypernormalisation of Information Systems Research
detail.abstract:
The Information Systems research discipline claims to build a cumulative Knowledge Base to inform practice, yet it is organised around a closed loop of self-referential simulation. We diagnose this state as hypernormalisation-a late-Soviet condition in which official rituals are meticulously performed despite a widespread recognition that they no longer map reliably onto lived reality. We identify four escalating mechanisms that sustain this institutional order: the Simulation of Accumulation, in which the journal article functions as a proof-of-work token; the Simulation of Relevance, in which "Implications for Practice" operate as rituals of displacement; the Simulation of Problem Solving, in which Design Science Research produces perpetual prototypes; and the Simulation of the Scholar, in which researchers inhabit a split subjectivity (Living Vnye). 

We argue that Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) constitutes the discipline's Glasnost moment. By automating the generation of methodologically fluent, theoretically compliant text at near-zero marginal cost, GenAI precipitates the collapse of the proof-of-work signalling economy not by attacking its institutions, but by exposing their performative nature. It renders the underlying logic visible, stripping the journal article of its value as a proxy for cognitive labour. Instead of offering renewal, this transparency forces a structural reweighting of epistemic authority: away from the mechanical production of form (Episteme), now inexpensive and abundant, toward judgment grounded in direct contact with reality (Phronesis) and exposure to consequence-a signal that cannot be sustained without the friction of the world.

title: Endogenous Technology Adoption in a Search Economy
affiliations: Saïd Business School, University of Oxford and University of Oxford, Saïd Business School

detail.title: Endogenous Technology Adoption in a Search Economy
detail.abstract: We develop a general-equilibrium model of endogenous technology adoption in an economy with product-market search frictions. Under frictional search, the static pricing game among heterogeneous firms producing the same variety yields variable markups represented by a gamma hazard function, resulting in within-variety profit dispersion that drives adoption incentives and economic growth—the mechanism absent under frictionless search. Strikingly, when imperfect search is the only friction, its degree does not affect growth, as the partial-equilibrium effect on markups is exactly offset by the general-equilibrium effect on demand. Incorporating additional features such as entry, search effort, and creative destruction creates a wedge between the two effects and allows search frictions to have dynamic implications. Our quantitative analysis of the U.S. economy shows that structural changes in search efficiency and the right tail of the productivity distribution over the past three decades have substantially raised welfare through technology adoption. The current U.S. productivity growth slowdown thus implies a sizable increase in adoption barriers.

reference: Peterson Institute for International Economics Policy Brief 26-5
title: Can Trump Keep his Tariffs if the Supreme Court Invalidates Them?
affiliations: Peterson Institute for International Economics

detail.title: Can Trump Keep his Tariffs if the Supreme Court Invalidates Them?

publicationDetails.detailsText: Peterson Institute for International Economics Policy Brief 26-5
publicationDetails.journalName: Peterson Institute for International Economics (PIIE) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
The Trump administration’s trade team has vowed to employ alternative legal strategies to keep its high tariff wall in place if the Supreme Court invalidates President Trump’s sweeping “reciprocal tariffs” by striking down his use of the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) to impose them. Wolff reviews the four possible tariff statutes that could be invoked— Sections 122, 338, 301, and 232—but they have major limitations. Each is either narrow, temporary, or specific, compared with IEEPA, and cannot be used to recreate Trump’s across-the-board tariff wall.

Key Takeaways

The administration’s next moves will depend on how the Supreme Court defines the president’s “emergency” powers to impose tariffs.

Tariffs imposed under section 122 have to be justified by a serious balance of payments problem and expire after 150 days unless Congress extends them.

Section 338 has not been invoked in 100 years and requires strong proof of discrimination against American goods.

Two other familiar statutes can be used only selectively but require findings of unfair foreign trade practices (section 301) or threats to national security (section 232).

reference: Kilts Center at Chicago Booth Marketing Data Center Paper
title: Got Chocolate Milk? The Effect of Flavored Milk Ban in Los Angeles on Retail Beverage Consumption
affiliations: University of Texas at Dallas - Naveen Jindal School of Management, University of Texas at Dallas - Naveen Jindal School of Management and University of Southern California, Marshall School of Business

detail.title: Got Chocolate Milk? The Effect of Flavored Milk Ban in Los Angeles on Retail Beverage Consumption

publicationDetails.detailsText: Kilts Center at Chicago Booth Marketing Data Center Paper
publicationDetails.journalName: Kilts Center at Chicago Booth Marketing Data Center Paper Series

detail.abstract: This study examines how local school nutrition policies influence household purchasing behavior outside the school setting. Using the 2011 flavored milk ban in the Los Angeles Unified School District, the authors test whether restricting a sugar-sweetened beverage in schools generates spillovers to beverage retail purchases. Leveraging retail scanner data and a synthetic control design, the analysis shows that retail purchases of flavored milk fell by about 8% in affected areas, indicating little household substitution for the in-school restriction. The decline was larger in markets with lower income and higher baseline consumption. The ban also prompted short-run substitution toward juice boxes, while purchases of plain milk and soda remained largely unchanged, suggesting limited cross-category displacement and a net decline in protein intake. Additional analyses rule out retailer pricing or promotional responses and show that the initial demand reduction occurred before school reopening, consistent with the policy operating primarily as an information shock amplified by negative publicity rather than by physical product displacement. This interpretation is further supported by the later policy repeal, which attracted little consumer attention and produced no retail spillovers. Overall, the findings show that school-based regulations can reshape retail demand through policy-induced publicity and health awareness.

title: The Value of Words: Evidence from Non-Financial Disclosure Regulation
affiliations: Bank of Italy, Bank of Italy, Bank of Italy, Bank of Italy and Bank of Italy

detail.title: The Value of Words: Evidence from Non-Financial Disclosure Regulation

publicationDetails.detailsText: Bank of Italy Temi di Discussione (Working Paper) No. 1498
publicationDetails.journalName: Bank of Italy Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: We examine the effects of less stringent non-financial disclosure regulation on operating costs and access to external financing for micro firms in Italy. Since 2016, firms below certain size thresholds have been exempt from filing reports with qualitative information that complements standard balance sheet items. Compliance rates were higher among older and more productive firms, in line with strategic considerations that play a role in influencing policy uptake. However, the benefits of simplified reporting appear limited: using a regression discontinuity design that exploits the multidimensional size cut-offs determining eligibility, we find no evidence of cost savings. Instead, we document a negative impact on ownership transfers and access to credit markets due to increased opacity, suggesting that reduced information disclosure to stakeholders may hinder business dynamism.

title: Principle-Based Marketing: A Conceptual Model (2026)

detail.title: Principle-Based Marketing: A Conceptual Model (2026)
detail.abstract: Organisations increasingly embed socially responsible practices into marketing strategies amid rising ESG imperatives and consumer demands, yet empirical inconsistencies persist due to scepticism, perceived hypocrisy, and backlash in polarised markets. While prior frameworks and reviews map CSR/CRM fundamentals they offer limited tactical guidance for conceptualising and delivering initiatives that balance moral legitimacy with ethical expectations. In response, this paper introduces Principle-Based Marketing (PBM) as a novel integrative framework and process model that uniquely positions enduring organisational principles as a consumer-centric fulcrum for aligning social values with marketing strategy. Synthesising disparate marketing schools of thought (exchange, macromarketing, consumer behaviour, management, service-dominant logic), corporate conduct theories, and marketplace dynamics, PBM proposes five interrelated constructs (objective commitment, cognisance, communication, internal congruence, and external congruence) that subsume granular variables to resolve empirical inconsistencies. Hypotheses delineate pathways from organisational actions to consumer perceptions, attitudes, and behaviours, yielding a managerial typology for risk assessment, brand differentiation, and portfolio audits. PBM advances current literature by providing theoretical parsimony and practical tools absent in existing syntheses, while addressing calls for holistic, actionable models in socially driven markets.

title: Willingness to Respond: Modeling Endogenous Termination in Discrete Choice Experiments
affiliations: HHL Leipzig Graduate School of Management, Goethe University Frankfurt - Department of Marketing and Copenhagen Business School - Department of Marketing

detail.title: Willingness to Respond: Modeling Endogenous Termination in Discrete Choice Experiments
detail.abstract: We introduce TRACE-Termination-Responsive Adjusted Choice Estimation-a new class of hierarchical Bayes models designed to correct for bias in discrete choice experiments caused by endogenous respondent dropout. Traditional models assume a fixed number of completed choice tasks per respondent, overlooking the possibility that some may terminate early for reasons related to their unobserved preferences, producing either a selection bias if early terminators are discarded or biased preference inferences if they are retained in the hierarchical model. TRACE addresses this issue by linking willingness-to-respond (WTR) to individual preferences. Through simulations and multiple empirical studies employing voluntary choice task designs, we demonstrate that standard hierarchical Bayes models systematically distort preference estimates when WTR is endogenous, while TRACE recovers unbiased preferences. Empirically, we find that WTR is often driven by the attractiveness of inside options and price sensitivity, though these effects vary by context. Combined with voluntary task designs and progressive incentive alignment, TRACE offers a novel methodology for conjoint analysis that respects respondents' decision on when to stop without compromising data quality. This framework supports unbiased estimates, enables more cost-efficient experimental designs, and opens new avenues for adapting choice tasks dynamically to maintain participant engagement.

title: Position: Balance Human Agency & AI Assistance in the Tussle for the Right to
affiliations: , Singapore University of Technology and Design (SUTD) - Information System Technology and Design, Singapore Management University, Nanyang Technological University, , , , Harvard University, , National University of Singapore (NUS) - Faculty of Law, National University of Singapore (NUS) - Department of Information Systems and Analytics and

detail.title: Position: Balance Human Agency & AI Assistance in the Tussle for the Right to

declarations.funderStatement: This research/project is supported by the National Research Foundation, Singapore under its AI Singapore Programme

detail.abstract: AI increasingly mediates daily life, offering efficiency and support, yet its technical properties risk subtly eroding human agency by undermining the ability to exercise meaningful discretion and decision making. We advance a rights-based framing centered on four everyday rights at stake in an AI-mediated world: the Rights to Learn, Work, Own, and Choose, which capture agency and decision making across education, labor, creative production, and leisure. We posit that AI systems should be designed and governed to actively balance human agency and AI assistance in this tussle for the Right to *. To operationalize this, we introduce output-oriented research questions that describe the behaviors and capacities AI systems should support in their deployment to preserve agency.

reference: MIT Center for Transportation & Logistics Research Paper No. 2025/036
title: Case Study: Workforce Planning in the Age of AI
affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Center for Transportation & Logistics, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Center for Transportation & Logistics and Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - School of Engineering

detail.title: Case Study: Workforce Planning in the Age of AI

publicationDetails.detailsText: MIT Center for Transportation & Logistics Research Paper No. 2025/036
publicationDetails.journalName: MIT Center for Transportation & Logistics Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
In 2024, ExampleState experienced the fastest population growth in the nation, placing unprecedented demands on the Company (ExampleCo) to deliver and maintain nearly 80,000 center-line miles of roadway (Company, 2024). Continued population growth, supply chain disruptions, and rising costs highlight the need for ExampleCo to operate more efficiently. To address these challenges, ExampleCo must analyze its internal operations in detail and strategically adopt emerging technologies to maintain economic resilience, support national commerce, and meet increasing mobility needs (Bureau of Transportation Statistics, 2023; Sheffi, 2025).

This report addresses ExampleCo leadership’s key questions about AI’s impact on the workforce. Where should ExampleCo deploy AI, what benefits are expected, and how will it affect the workforce? To answer these questions, we introduce a new methodology that breaks jobs into their basic units: tasks. For each task, we evaluate its cost and assess to what extent it can be accelerated by an AI-based system. This task-based framework allows for a precise assessment of AI’s impact across roles, departments, and the organization. This research was conducted at the MIT Center for Transportation & Logistics, with a focus on artificial intelligence, labor economics, and supply chain management. The report provides data-driven insights to support ExampleCo’s strategic decisions regarding AI’s impact and investment.

title: A Spatially Aware Poisson Random Forest for Modelling Road Traffic Fatalities in Low- and Middle-Income Country Urban Systems
affiliations: Stellenbosch University and Stellenbosch University

detail.title: A Spatially Aware Poisson Random Forest for Modelling Road Traffic Fatalities in Low- and Middle-Income Country Urban Systems
detail.abstract: Accurate modelling of road traffic fatalities in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) is challenged by count-based outcomes, spatial dependence, and complex non-linear interactions between infrastructure, exposure, and socio-economic context. Classical Poisson and Negative Binomial regression models provide interpretable frameworks but are limited by restrictive functional assumptions, while standard machine-learning approaches often ignore the statistical properties of count data and spatial structure. This paper introduces a Spatially Aware Poisson Random Forest (SAPRF) model that integrates Poisson deviance–based learning, ensemble methods, and spatial encoding to address these limitations. Using geocoded road fatality data from Gauteng Province, South Africa (2015–2019), SAPRF is evaluated against Poisson regression, Negative Binomial regression, and a standard Random Forest. Results show that SAPRF substantially improves predictive accuracy and calibration for low-count outcomes, reducing mean absolute error by approximately 30–40% relative to benchmark models while also reducing spatial clustering of residuals. Feature importance and partial dependence analyses demonstrate the model’s ability to capture meaningful non-linear interactions involving intersection proximity, temporal exposure, traffic volume, and spatial context. The findings position SAPRF as a robust and transferable modelling framework for crash-frequency analysis in complex urban systems, particularly in LMIC contexts characterised by spatial heterogeneity and data constraints.

title: Human-ADS Collaboration in Automated HGV Operations: Part I – Revealing Divergences of LLM-simulated and Human Takeover Decision-making
affiliations: Monash University, Monash University, Research Institute of Highway Ministry of Transport, Central South University and Monash University

detail.title: Human-ADS Collaboration in Automated HGV Operations: Part I – Revealing Divergences of LLM-simulated and Human Takeover Decision-making
detail.abstract: Global adoption of Level-3 autonomous driving systems (ADS) in commercial heavy goods vehicles (HGVs) remains limited, as concerns about reliability and safety foster trust miscalibration and reinforce experience-dependent risk heuristics. This study examines human–ADS interaction in HGV operations and investigates whether large language models (LLMs) can generate takeover decisions that resemble human behavior. Human-in-the-loop experiments were conducted within the fully compiled CARLA simulation platform featuring a large-scale road environment (30 × 30 km²) with realistic background traffic flow dynamics. Human reactions, particularly takeover behavior during ADS operations, were systematically examined from compliance rates, decision latency, intervention strategies, and crash outcomes across freeway merging, freeway navigating, and urban driving scenarios. The same scenarios were presented to LLM-agent-equipped HGVs, where the agents were trained as scalable surrogates for “truck drivers”, and their performance was then recorded and compared with human counterparts. Results showed that (i) crash rates dropped substantially from human participants (12.0%) to LLM-agent-controlled ADS (2.8%–4.6%); (ii) whereas LLM agents relied exclusively on deceleration and steering for safety responses, human participants also frequently used acceleration as a preferred intervention strategy; and (iii) participants with 6–20 years of driving experience intervened more pre-emptively and exhibited below 50% compliance with ADS operation. These findings suggest that human takeover decisions are shaped by experience-based risk heuristics and exhibit substantial heterogeneity across drivers. They also indicate that current LLMs are not yet reliable proxies for human supervisory behavior during the autonomous driving. The methodological framework developed in this investigation offers a replicable approach for researchers examining human-ADS interaction across transportation domains, and the empirical findings inform appropriate boundaries for LLM application in safety-critical human factors research.

title: Local Labour Market Conditions and Electoral Behaviour: An Instrumental Variable Approach from Italy
affiliations: Bank of Italy and Banca d’Italia

detail.title: Local Labour Market Conditions and Electoral Behaviour: An Instrumental Variable Approach from Italy

publicationDetails.detailsText: Bank of Italy Temi di Discussione (Working Paper) No. 1495
publicationDetails.journalName: Bank of Italy Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: What is the causal impact of local employment dynamics on electoral behaviour? We combine Italian labour market area-level data for four national elections (2008, 2013, 2018 and 2022) with a shift-share IV estimation design to identify how local labour market conditions, captured by changes in the employment rate, affect voter participation and incumbent support. Our baseline estimates show that a 1 p.p. drop in the employment rate yields a significant 0.76 p.p. increase in turnout and a 0.80 p.p. decline in incumbent vote share. Further analyses reveal crucial nuances. First, exploring mediation, we find that higher turnout in response to worsening labour market conditions accounts for roughly one-quarter of the total negative impact on incumbent support via a participation channel. Second, the effects appear to be driven entirely by adverse conditions: we find strong electoral reactions in areas actually experiencing employment declines, but no significant response where conditions improve, consistent with a protest voting framework. Third, while regional-national partisan alignment slightly moderates effect magnitudes, national accountability for economic performance largely dominates the local electoral reaction.

reference: Bank of Italy Temi di Discussione (Working Paper) No. 1500
title: What Drives Policy Rate Expectations? Evidence from the Post-Pandemic Monetary Policy Cycle
affiliations: Bank of Italy and Bank of Italy

detail.title: What Drives Policy Rate Expectations? Evidence from the Post-Pandemic Monetary Policy Cycle

publicationDetails.detailsText: Bank of Italy Temi di Discussione (Working Paper) No. 1500
publicationDetails.journalName: Bank of Italy Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: We investigate how demand and supply shocks, as perceived by markets, shaped revisions in expected ECB and Fed policy rates during the post-pandemic monetary policy cycle. To this end, we construct a measure of revisions in near-term policy rate expectations and embed it in a two-country daily BVAR model identified through sign and magnitude restrictions. Three patterns emerge. First, both central banks were perceived as more responsive to inflation than in the pre-ELB period, under both demand and supply shocks. Second, supply shocks were seen as being treated similarly to demand shocks, reflecting a lower perceived tolerance for supply-driven inflation. Third, supply shocks became a new source of cross-border spillovers in rate expectations. These findings point to a reconfiguration of perceived central bank reaction functions in high-inflation environments, when the risk of expectations de-anchoring becomes material.

reference: Bank of Italy Temi di Discussione (Working Paper) No. 1497
title: Safer Trade Among Democracies? Downward Trade Volatility and Political Regimes (1962-2018)
affiliations: Bank of Italy

detail.title: Safer Trade Among Democracies? Downward Trade Volatility and Political Regimes (1962-2018)

publicationDetails.detailsText: Bank of Italy Temi di Discussione (Working Paper) No. 1497
publicationDetails.journalName: Bank of Italy Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper examines the trade relations of the G7 countries from 1962 to 2018, categorising trade partners based on their political systems. First, it analyses trade openness depending on whether partners are democracies. Second, the paper introduces a trade risk measure related to a partner’s political system, defined as the downward volatility of trade flows. This measure accounts for both the likelihood and severity of potential trade disruptions. The study finds that trade among democracies has shown less downward volatility than trade with non-democratic regimes. This finding continues to hold even after accounting for important characteristics of the trading partners, such as their level of development and the types of goods traded (primary products, manufactured goods, or exports). The lower volatility associated with democratic regimes is likely due to stronger institutional limits on executive power, which may lead to more stable policies and business environments.

title: Fragmentation in European Equity Markets since 2019
affiliations: European Securities and Markets Authority, European Securities and Markets Authority and European Securities and Markets Authority

detail.title: Fragmentation in European Equity Markets since 2019
detail.abstract: Enacting the single European financial market, particularly through MiFID and MiFIR legislation, has shaped equity trading over the past decade. Recently, Brexit has led to a substantial reduction in securities trading within the remaining single market, with its long-term impact still evolving. Making use of regulatory data in a regression model, we estimate the evolution of the European share market microstructure from 2019 to 2022, with a specific focus on the impact of the UK withdrawal from Europe, given its pivotal role in equity markets. Our findings underscore a post-Brexit landscape marked by reduced fragmentation, heightened on-exchange trading, and diminished activity on systematic internalisers or over-the-counter. Furthermore, we observe that during market stress, fragmentation decreases slightly,-to-transparency" behaviour observed in the economic literature. The results of the analysis are also relevant in the context of European regulatory initiatives such as the Savings and Investments Union (SIU), to create an integrated and competitive financial market.

reference: Bank of Italy Temi di Discussione (Working Paper) No. 1499
title: Cui Prodest? The Heterogeneous Impact of Green Bonds on Companies’ ESG Score
affiliations: Bank of Italy and Bank of Italy

detail.title: Cui Prodest? The Heterogeneous Impact of Green Bonds on Companies’ ESG Score

publicationDetails.detailsText: Bank of Italy Temi di Discussione (Working Paper) No. 1499
publicationDetails.journalName: Bank of Italy Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: With the aim of providing a comprehensive framework of analysis, this paper develops a signalling model in which green bonds enable companies to disclose the adoption of clean production processes. Given that investors exhibit environmental preferences, companies that rely on green technologies benefit from lower financing costs and are able to improve their environmental performance. Specifically, green bonds encourage more polluting companies to start transitioning towards cleaner production. Using a large global sample of companies and a difference-in-differences strategy, we successfully test the model’s implications. The analysis also reveals that green bonds issued to finance mitigation activities are the most effective in improving companies’ environmental performance. In line with the model’s predictions, these bonds display the largest yield differential (greenium) compared with their conventional counterparts.

title: Comment on `What's the Matter with Tie-Breaking: Improving Efficiency in School Choice'

detail.title: Comment on `What's the Matter with Tie-Breaking: Improving Efficiency in School Choice'
detail.abstract: The code that was used in Erdil and Ergin (2008) to compute stable improvement cycles sometimes generated unstable matchings. I identify the minor bug in their code that caused this issue, and I present a corrected implementation. While the general insights from the computational experiments obtained by Erdil and Ergin (2008) persist, the true fraction of improving students is slightly smaller than reported, while their average improvement in rank is larger than reported. All theoretical findings in Erdil and Ergin (2008) are unaffected.

title: Minimum Wages and the Rise of the Robots
affiliations: National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER), University of British Columbia (UBC), Halle Institute for Economic Research,  and Stanford

detail.title: Minimum Wages and the Rise of the Robots
detail.abstract: This paper studies how minimum wage policy affects firms' adoption of automation technologies. Using both state-level measures of robot exposure and novel plant-level data on industrial robot imports linked to U.S. Census microdata from 1992-2021, we show that increases in minimum wages raise the likelihood of robot adoption in manufacturing. Our preferred identification exploits discontinuities at state borders, comparing otherwise similar firms exposed to different wage floors. Across specifications, a 10 percent increase in the minimum wage increases robot adoption by roughly 8 percent relative to the mean.

reference: Bank of Italy Temi di Discussione (Working Paper) No. 1496
title: Natural Disasters and Markups
affiliations: Bank of Italy and Bank of Italy

detail.title: Natural Disasters and Markups

publicationDetails.detailsText: Bank of Italy Temi di Discussione (Working Paper) No. 1496
publicationDetails.journalName: Bank of Italy Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Can firm-level markup adjustments affect the aggregate cost of large, localized shocks? Using firm-level data from Italy, we show that natural disasters lead to a persistent decline in markups among affected manufacturing firms. We apply an oligopolistic competition model with idiosyncratic shocks directly to firm-level data and invert it to recover productivity for firms impacted by the 2012 Northern Italy earthquake. We then quantify how markup adjustments shape aggregate manufacturing productivity and welfare. Our baseline results suggest that markup changes amplified the aggregate productivity and welfare losses of the earthquake by approximately 20%.

reference: New England Law | Boston Research Paper Forthcoming
title: JPE 2.0: A Modern Approach to Evaluating Judicial Performance
affiliations: New England Law | Boston and University of Denver - Institute for the Advancement of the American Legal System

detail.title: JPE 2.0: A Modern Approach to Evaluating Judicial Performance

publicationDetails.detailsText: New England Law | Boston Research Paper Forthcoming
publicationDetails.journalName: New England Law | Boston Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This article shares the results of a multi-year, national effort to modernize judicial performance evaluation (JPE) programs, which are currently in use or under consideration in nearly twenty U.S. jurisdictions. In particular, it describes the genesis and work of the JPE 2.0 Project, a national effort undertaken by IAALS, the Institute for the Advancement of the American Legal System at the University of Denver. The article presents new findings on the current state of JPE programs and offers recommendations on how such programs can provide more reliable data on judicial performance, include the views of a broader range of court users, and better reflect the roles and responsibilities of the modern judiciary.

title: Assessing the Effectiveness of Climate Communication Strategies on Low-Carbon Milk Choice: A Comparison of Priming, Information, and Affective Slogans
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Maine, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Michigan State University

detail.title: Assessing the Effectiveness of Climate Communication Strategies on Low-Carbon Milk Choice: A Comparison of Priming, Information, and Affective Slogans
detail.abstract: Carbon labels are widely used tools to guide low-carbon consumption, thereby mitigating climate change. However, their effectiveness in emerging markets is constrained by consumers’ limited familiarity and concerns about label credibility. Using milk as a focal product, we conduct an online discrete choice experiment in China to examine the effectiveness of carbon labels and how they can be promoted through targeted climate communication strategies. Specifically, this paper aims to (i) estimate  consumers’ WTP for the carbon reduction label and examine how they trade off this altruistic attribute against organic certification (semi-altruistic) and nutrition claims (private benefits); (ii) compare effects of different climate communication strategies, including priming, information, and information plus slogan, which represent a conceptual escalation in message content and persuasive depth; and (iii) test whether the blockchain-verified carbon-reduction label leads to higher WTP than the plain carbon-reduction label, and whether the effects of communication treatments diminish when applied to the blockchain-verified version. The findings reveal that, first, in the control group, WTP for plain carbon-reduction label is broadly comparable to nutrition and organic attributes, though lower by roughly 17-19%. Adding blockchain verification substantially increases its WTP, making it the most valued attribute. Secondly, priming does not meaningfully change preferences, information elevates WTP for the plain carbon-reduction label, and information plus slogan produces the most significant increase for that label. However, no treatments further shift WTP for the blockchain-verified carbon-reduction label, indicating a ceiling effect. Those results provide policy implications for enhancing the effectiveness of carbon labeling.

title: Foreign Direct Investment and Greenhouse Gas Emissions: Evidence across Income Groups and Technological Contexts
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, California State University, Dominguez Hills, California State University Dominguez Hills and California State University Dominguez Hills

detail.title: Foreign Direct Investment and Greenhouse Gas Emissions: Evidence across Income Groups and Technological Contexts
detail.abstract: This paper examines the impact of foreign direct investment (FDI) on greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions using both static and dynamic panel data models. To capture heterogeneity across countries, we incorporate interaction terms in the system GMM estimations, focusing on middle- and high-income groups. The results indicate that FDI is positively associated with GHG emissions, suggesting that greater foreign investment tends to exacerbate environmental pressures. Furthermore, the analysis of sector-specific green patents reveals heterogeneous and often time-dependent effects that vary by technology type. In contrast, aggregate patent activity shows either positive or statistically insignificant relationships with emissions. Dynamic panel estimations confirm the persistent and robust positive linkage between FDI and GHG emissions across income groups, with somewhat stronger effects observed in middle-income economies. These findings underscore the need for targeted environmental policies that align the composition of FDI with sustainable development objectives and strengthen institutional frameworks in host countries.

title: Towards representative environmental asset management: an integrative framework for handling protest respondents in contingent valuation
affiliations: University of Murcia and Murcia University

detail.title: Towards representative environmental asset management: an integrative framework for handling protest respondents in contingent valuation
detail.abstract: Accurate economic valuation of environmental assets is critical for informed decision-making and sustainable resource management. Although Contingent Valuation (CV) studies serve as a valuable instrument for this purpose, their efficacy is frequently compromised by the presence of Protest Respondents (PRs). Traditionally, these individuals are excluded from analysis, introducing a potential selection bias that threatens the representativeness of welfare estimates. This study develops a comprehensive methodological to identify and integrate PRs using a case study of renewable electricity valuation.The research employs an overview of tools of missing data analysis to characterize the survey, which resulted in a definitive rejection of the missing completely at random hypothesis, highlighting the imperative inclusion of PRs to avoid significant bias in Willingness To Pay (WTP) estimates. Consequently, the study evaluates and compares different estimation techniques under two primary missing data scenarios, such as multiple imputation for missing at random and Heckman and double hurdle models for missing not at random.Results indicate that the missing not at random hypothesis is the most plausible in CV studies. Then, PRs possess a higher latent WTP compared to market participants, with estimates ranging from €7.62 (double hurdle) to €8.23 (Heckman), significantly exceeding the biased market participants of €6.42. The double hurdle model emerged as the most robust technique due to its resilience against the inherent unpredictability of protest behaviour. These findings establish a research foundation for informing more socially representative policy design and demonstrate that incorporating PRs is essential for accurate cost-benefit analysis in environmental asset management.
